Miles Davis was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and composer whose restless innovation transformed jazz repeatedly across five decades, from cool jazz to modal jazz to rock fusion.

He pioneered cool jazz in the late nineteen-forties, a reaction against bebop's virtuosic intensity, featuring intricate orchestrations and a more reserved aesthetic. In 1959, Davis released "Kind of Blue," the best-selling jazz album of all time, which introduced modal improvisation and redefined how jazz musicians approached harmonic structure.

He led the First Great Quintet from 1964 to 1968 featuring John Coltrane, and later the Second Great Quintet from 1965 to 1968 whose rhythmically complex interplay reshaped ensemble jazz. His distinctive muted trumpet tone and ability to play minimally, letting silence speak, redefined trumpet aesthetics for generations.

Davis ventured into rock fusion with "Bitches Brew" in 1970, incorporating electric instruments and funk grooves to reach broader audiences and influence both jazz and rock musicians. Throughout his career, he worked across styles—bebop, hard bop, modal jazz, fusion—perpetually reinventing himself rather than repeating past successes.

He was influenced by Louis Armstrong, whose solo innovations he built upon and reinterpreted in modern contexts, and by Duke Ellington, whose compositional sophistication influenced his bandleading approach. He absorbed the harmonic language of Charlie Parker, the bebop pioneer, before moving beyond it. With John Coltrane, his saxophonist in his classic quintet, Davis created music whose harmonic innovations complemented his sparse melodicism.
